prompt: A small hot-sauce brand reviews last month's social activity. Sort each item into paid, owned or earned media.

cards.text: A recipe reel posted on the brand's own profile.
cards.explanation: The brand published it on its own channel, at no media cost.

cards.text: A weekly update sent to the brand's broadcast channel subscribers.
cards.explanation: Broadcast channels the brand runs are owned media.

cards.text: A catalog carousel bought in the auction manager to reach non-followers who like spicy food.
cards.explanation: It was bought through the platform's self-serve auction to reach non-followers.

cards.text: A sponsored vertical video shown to food lovers in three cities.
cards.explanation: A sponsored in-feed video is paid media.

cards.text: A customer's unprompted taste-test video that friends share widely.
cards.explanation: Voluntary, uncompensated mentions cannot be bought directly.

cards.text: A community thread where strangers argue about which of its sauces is hottest.
cards.explanation: Organic community discussion is earned media.

question_text: A pottery student with 40 followers posts a short wheel-throwing video that most early viewers watch to the end. On the same day, a homeware chain with 900,000 followers posts a product clip that most early viewers skip. On an interest-graph video platform, what should we expect?
hint: Ask what the interest graph uses to decide distribution.
correct_answer_citation: In an interest-graph feed (pioneered at scale by short-form vertical video platforms), an account with zero followers can achieve massive organic distribution if its video holds viewer attention in early test cohorts.

options.option_text: The chain's clip reaches far more people, because reach follows follower count.
options.option_explanation: That describes a social-graph feed. Here follower count guarantees little reach.

options.option_text: Both reach about the same number of people, because each is shown only to its followers.
options.option_explanation: An interest graph distributes content independent of whether the viewer follows the creator.

options.option_text: The student's video can reach far more people, because it held attention in early test viewers.
options.option_explanation: Correct. Watch time in early cohorts, not followers, drives distribution.

options.option_text: Neither is distributed, because the platform waits for likes from followers.
options.option_explanation: Interest-graph ranking leans on watch time, replays, shares and comments from any viewer.

prompt: A sleep-mask brand plans its paid social campaigns. Place each ad in the funnel stage it serves.

cards.text: A broad-audience video about lying awake at 3 a.m. under streetlight glare.
cards.explanation: A narrative hook introducing the problem to cold audiences.

cards.text: Five short opening hooks tested on people who have never visited the store.
cards.explanation: Prospecting creative aimed at cold audiences.

cards.text: A blackout demonstration shown to people who watched the 3 a.m. video.
cards.explanation: Demonstrations go to users who engaged with prospecting content.

cards.text: A comparison carousel of the mask against foam earplugs, shown to profile visitors.
The exact silk mask and its current price, pulled from the catalog feed for cart abandoners.
cards.explanation: Dynamic product ads use the catalog feed to retarget high-intent users.

cards.text: A personalized 10 percent offer on the colour a site visitor viewed twice.
cards.explanation: Personalized SKUs and promotions for high-intent visitors are bottom-of-funnel.

question_text: A climbing-chalk brand compares two creators for the same fee. Creator A has 600,000 followers, and her recent videos average 9,000 views with generic one-word comments. Creator B has 25,000 followers who are mostly climbers, and his videos average 14,000 views with detailed gear questions. Which choice follows good partner selection?
hint: Look past the follower totals to the signals marketers audit.
correct_answer_citation: Selecting creator partners by follower count alone is a classic digital marketing error, because follower totals can be inflated by inactive accounts or bots. Marketers instead audit audience demographic fit, comment quality, average view-to-follower ratios, and past conversion performance.

options.option_text: Creator A, because 600,000 followers guarantees broader reach.
options.option_explanation: Her views are only 1.5 percent of her followers, and the comments suggest inactive or bot accounts.

options.option_text: Creator B, because his audience fits, his comments are substantive and his views are over half his followers.
options.option_explanation: Correct. Audience fit, comment quality and view-to-follower ratio all favour B.

options.option_text: Creator A, because macro-influencers always have higher engagement rates.
options.option_explanation: Macro-influencers typically have lower average engagement rates.

options.option_text: Either one, because parasocial trust depends only on how often a creator posts.
options.option_explanation: Parasocial trust grows over time, but partner selection still requires auditing the audience.

prompt: A homeware brand describes four moments in its social commerce work. Name the concept each one shows.

cases.text: When a lamp sells out in the warehouse, its stock count inside the social app drops to zero within seconds through an API link.
cases.explanation: The merchant's PIM and OMS sync inventory and pricing with the in-app shop.

cases.text: A viewer taps the throw blanket in a living-room photo, picks the grey one and pays with a card saved in the app.
cases.explanation: A shoppable tag lets the viewer select and pay in two taps.

cases.text: A host demonstrates a kettle on camera, answers chat questions, and announces a coupon that expires in ten minutes.
cases.explanation: Live video, chat, demonstration and a time-limited coupon make livestream shopping.

cases.text: Orders double, but the brand receives no email addresses for the new buyers and pays a commission on each sale.
cases.explanation: The platform keeps the checkout, charges commission and restricts the customer data passed back.

prompt: A brand considers a clearly disclosed virtual influencer for several products. Sort each product by how well a virtual endorser fits it.

cards.text: Designer sunglasses for a summer lookbook.
cards.explanation: A symbolic, fashion-oriented product does not rely on physical sensory trust.

cards.text: A collectible outfit for a video game character.
cards.explanation: A symbolic product that a synthetic persona can model.

cards.text: A mattress claimed to ease lower-back pain.
cards.explanation: The claim depends on a body that felt the relief.

cards.text: A probiotic said to settle digestion.
cards.explanation: A credence good: buyers rely on trust that someone experienced the effect.

cards.text: Running insoles that reduce knee strain.
cards.explanation: An AI persona cannot authentically claim relief from joint pain.
